lead: The cockpit is a human-machine interface (HMI): the place where the crew senses the aircraft's state, decides and acts. Good cockpit design fits displays, controls and alerts to human limits of attention, memory and reaction time, so that normal flying is easy and a failure is obvious. Some syllabi leave this chapter out, so it is kept short.
prereq: You need: Electronic displays: PFD, MFD, EADI and EHSI.

sections.h3: Layout: the most urgent data nearest the eyes

blocks.text: The crew works in a loop: sense, decide, act. Displays feed the sensing, controls carry the action and alerts interrupt when something is wrong. Information hierarchy decides position: primary flight data sits in the primary field of view straight ahead, navigation and system pages sit beside it, and rarely used data sits on overhead panels or in menus. Controls follow the same rule. Fighters put the most used switches on the stick and throttle (HOTAS). Every control must show its state, by its position, a light or a display echo.

Airbus uses a dark cockpit philosophy: with every system normal, no overhead light is on, so any light that comes on means a change. Certification asks the same of all large aeroplanes: under CS 25.1302 and the matching FAA rule, the crew must be able to detect, understand and act on the information each system gives, without the design itself causing errors.

Alerts come in levels. A warning needs immediate action (fire, stall, terrain) and comes with a red master warning light and an aural alert. A caution needs timely action (a generator failure) and comes in amber with a master caution light. Lower levels inform without demanding action. Colour must never be the only cue: a word, a shape or a sound must carry the same meaning, because sunlight washes out colours and some pilots have weak colour vision. A master caution that flashes for trivial faults teaches the crew to ignore it.

Mode awareness means the crew always knows what the automation is doing and what it will do next. The flight mode annunciator shows active modes in one colour and armed modes in another. A silent mode change, or two modes that look alike on the screen, is a design fault that has contributed to accidents.

examples.question: A pilot scans six display areas in a fixed loop, spending 0.4 s on each. A new caution appears on one area only, and the crew must notice it within 1.5 s. (a) Find the time for one full scan. (b) Find the worst-case wait before the eyes reach the caution. (c) Find the average wait if the caution can appear at any moment. (d) Does a caution shown only on that area meet the 1.5 s need?
steps: Worst case: the caution appears just as the eyes leave that area. They return after the other five areas: 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 s.
Average: for 0.4 s of each 2.4 s cycle the eyes are already on the area (wait 0). For the other 2.0 s the wait falls evenly from 2.0 s to 0, averaging 1.0 s. Average = (2.0 ÷ 2.4) × 1.0 = 0.83 s.
The average (0.83 s) meets 1.5 s but the worst case (2.0 s) does not, and the design must meet the worst case.
Fix: a master caution light in the primary field of view and an aural chime catch the eye wherever it is.
examples.answer: Scan 2.4 s; worst-case wait 2.0 s; average 0.83 s. A caution shown only on that area fails the 1.5 s need in the worst case, so it needs a master caution light and a sound.

traps: Writing that more data on the screen is better HMI. Clutter lengthens the scan and hides the abnormal value.
Blaming every mode confusion on the pilot. A silent or look-alike mode change is a design failure.
Taking the full scan time as the worst-case wait. The worst case is the scan time minus one dwell.

quiz.a: The interface between the crew and the aircraft systems: displays, controls and alerts.

quiz.q: What is the dark cockpit philosophy?
quiz.a: With all systems normal, no overhead light is on, so any light that comes on shows a change.

quiz.q: Why must colour never be the only cue?
quiz.a: Sunlight washes out colour and some pilots have weak colour vision, so a word, shape or sound must carry the same meaning.

quiz.q: Five areas at 0.5 s each. Find the scan time and the worst-case wait.
Explain mode confusion and give two design fixes.
quiz.a: The crew believes the automation is in one mode while it is in another. Fixes: show active and armed modes clearly on the FMA and box every change; avoid look-alike mode labels; alert on an unexpected mode reversion.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cockpit designers test layouts in simulators with eye tracking to measure real scan paths, and touchscreen cockpits raise new questions about use in turbulence. Accident reports are the best reading on HMI. Search for 'CS 25.1302', 'mode awareness', 'alert fatigue' and 'eye tracking flight deck'.

spec.aria: A timeline from 0 to 2.8 seconds divided into seven 0.4 second dwells: EICAS, PFD, ND, outside, MCP, overhead and EICAS again. A caution appears at 0.4 seconds as the eyes leave EICAS and is seen at 2.4 seconds when they return, a worst-case wait of 2.0 seconds. A second arrow shows the need: seen within 1.5 seconds. A note gives the average wait of 0.83 seconds.
